summary: Extends IPFIX, used to export flow data from measurement devices, so the properties of the IPFIX Information Model, such as data types, can be encoded within the message stream. A collector can then interpret new elements without outside documentation.

eli5.summary: Data about traffic arrives as numbers. This lets the sender include a note saying what kind of number each one is.

questions: how to export enterprise specific ipfix elements
what is an ipfix options template
subtitle: How an IPFIX exporter can describe its own custom data fields inside the message stream.

tldr.problem: IPFIX templates only tell a collector the size of each field, so a collector cannot decode enterprise-specific Information Elements it has never heard of and must treat them as opaque octets.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5610 defines eight new Information Elements and an Options Template that lets the exporter send type records saying each element's name, data type, semantics, units, range and description.
tldr.outcome: Collectors and IPFIX Files can store, display and do limited analysis on unfamiliar elements. It does not replace registering useful elements with IANA.

today: RFC 5610 is a Proposed Standard from July 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says it is not a substitute for registering useful Information Elements with IANA.

sections.title: The Problem With Opaque Fields
sections.content:
IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) describes each Data Record with a Template: a list of Information Elements taken from an IANA registry. But a Template encodes only the size of each field. It carries no full type information, although the IPFIX Information Model in RFC 5102 defines such information for registered elements.

This mostly hurts enterprise-specific Information Elements. Analysis tools built without advance knowledge of them can only treat and store their values as opaque octet arrays. With richer information, efficient storage, display and limited analysis become possible even for a Collecting Process that was not written to understand those elements.

RFC 5610 therefore defines a way to encode the properties of Information Elements inline in an IPFIX Message stream using IPFIX Options, with no external reference or out-of-band configuration.
sections.eli5: If a sender uses a made-up kind of number, the receiver only sees a pile of bytes. This RFC lets the sender explain what each pile means.

sections.title: Scope and Standardization
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that this is not a replacement for registering generally useful Information Elements with IANA. The mechanism adds overhead and does not give the real interoperability that standardization does, so the authors highly recommend standardizing all new generally useful elements. The type information needed here is a good basis for the description a registration requires.

If an element once described this way later becomes IANA-registered, old and new versions can coexist, and translating between them is out of scope. The document relies on RFC 5101 (the IPFIX Protocol) for terminology and encodings and on RFC 5102 for data types and semantics.
sections.eli5: The note-passing trick is for private, custom numbers. If a number is useful to everybody, it should go in the official list instead.

sections.title: The New Information Elements
sections.content:
The type records are built from eight Information Elements defined here. IANA assigned them numbers 339 to 346.

  • informationElementDataType (339): the abstract data type, with values 0 to 19 from octetArray to ipv6Address.
  • informationElementDescription (340): a UTF-8 human-readable description. It MAY carry in-line language tags, and without one the i-default language SHOULD be assumed.
  • informationElementName (341): a UTF-8 name used as a simple identifier.
  • informationElementRangeBegin (342) and informationElementRangeEnd (343): the inclusive low and high ends of acceptable values.
  • informationElementSemantics (344): values 0 to 5, from default to flags.
  • informationElementUnits (345): values 0 to 12, from none to entries.
  • privateEnterpriseNumber (346): scopes the properties to a specific enterprise element.

The record also needs informationElementId from RFC 5477, which can refer only to IANA-defined elements. To describe an enterprise-specific element, the exporter sends the enterprise number in privateEnterpriseNumber and the element number with the Enterprise bit cleared in informationElementId. The collector MUST ignore that Enterprise bit. For an IANA element, the enterprise number is 0 or is omitted.
sections.eli5: Each note has slots: what the number is called, what kind of number it is, what it measures, and what range it can have.

sections.title: The Type Options Template
sections.content:
An Information Element Type Options Template attaches type information to the elements used in Templates, scoped to an Observation Domain within a Transport Session. Records it describes are called Information Element type records. The template SHOULD contain informationElementId and privateEnterpriseNumber, which MUST both be Scope Fields, plus data type, semantics, units, range begin, range end, name and description. Units SHOULD be omitted for a unitless quantity or a non-quantity, range ends SHOULD be omitted when the data type already defines them, and the description MAY be omitted for export efficiency.

Where cross-vendor interoperability matters, an Exporting Process using enterprise-specific elements SHOULD export a type record for each one. Collectors MAY use them to handle unknown elements better. Exporters using enterprise elements for proprietary features MAY omit them.

Type records are scoped to the Transport Session and are not a way to define elements permanently. Exporters SHOULD NOT export records that duplicate information the collector can reasonably be assumed to have, such as for IANA elements.
sections.eli5: The sender first announces the form for the notes, then sends one filled-in note per custom number. The notes only count for this one conversation.

sections.title: Consistency and Valid Combinations
sections.content:
Once a type record has been exported for an element within a Transport Session, all later type records for it MUST be identical, and duplicates in a given Observation Domain SHOULD be avoided. Type information MUST NOT be redefined by type records, and a collector MUST NOT let a record replace its own internal definition. An element with conflicting semantic or type information MUST be ignored.

Not every pairing of data type and semantics is valid. Any semantics are valid for the unsigned types. Any except flags are valid for the signed types. Any except identifier or flags are valid for float32 and float64. All other types allow only default. Exporters MUST NOT send invalid combinations, and collectors MUST ignore them.
sections.eli5: Once a note says what a number is, it cannot change its mind. Also, some labels make no sense together, like calling an address a counter.

sections.title: Worked Example: TCP Flags
sections.content:
The appendix uses two example private elements: initialTCPFlags (private IE 14, 1 octet), the TCP flags on the first TCP packet of the flow, and unionTCPFlags (private IE 15, 1 octet), the union of the flags on all later packets. A normal Template with these elements gives a collector no hint that they hold flags.

To fix that, the exporter first sends the Type Options Template, then two type records. Each record gives the enterprise number, the element number, the data type unsigned8 (0x01), the semantics flags (0x05) and the element name. A collector now knows to treat the byte as a set of flags.
sections.eli5: A mystery byte arrives. The note says it is a row of on and off switches, so the receiver knows to read it as switches rather than as a plain number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5101 apply. In addition, the precedence rules (a collector's own knowledge wins, and types cannot be redefined during a session) are designed to limit the chance that an attacker maliciously redefines the data model.

The name and description are strings. IPFIX strings are length-prefixed and UTF-8 encoded, which reduces the risk of unterminated-string attacks, but collectors should still be careful converting to null-terminated strings. Exporters MUST NOT export, and collectors MUST ignore, any name or description containing a null character (U+0000). The maximum IPFIX string length is 65512 octets, so either string can in principle be that long.
sections.eli5: Receivers should not let a note rewrite what they already know, and should reject notes with sneaky blank characters inside the text.

items.label: default
items.desc: No semantics apply; the value cannot be manipulated by a collector that does not understand it in advance.

items.label: quantity
items.desc: The quantity semantics value, defined in the IPFIX Information Model.

items.label: totalCounter
items.desc: The total counter semantics value, defined in the IPFIX Information Model.

items.label: deltaCounter
items.desc: The delta counter semantics value, defined in the IPFIX Information Model.

items.label: identifier
items.desc: The identifier semantics value, defined in the IPFIX Information Model.
